intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 (SMABF2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ASCC1 gene (614215) on chromosome 10q22.1.

checks.claim: Spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 (SMABF2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ASCC1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified homozygous and compound-heterozygous nonsense and frameshift TRIP4 and ASCC1 mutations that led to a truncation or the entire absence of the respective proteins and cosegregated with the disease phenotype.
checks.explanation: Abstract reports both zygosities across TRIP4 and ASCC1 combined; it does not specify that ASCC1 alone had both, nor name SMABF2.

checks.claim: The ASCC1 gene is located on chromosome 10q22.1.
checks.evidence_quote: We report on recessive loss-of-function mutations in two genes (TRIP4 and ASCC1)
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature restating the gene identified.

paragraphs.text: Spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 (SMABF2) is a severe neuromuscular disorder that begins before birth. Affected individuals have prenatal-onset muscle weakness or spinal muscular atrophy, neonatal hypotonia, multiple congenital contractures (arthrogryposis multiplex congenita), respiratory distress, and congenital bone fractures (Knierim et al., 2016; Bohm et al., 2019).

paragraphs.text: Oliveira et al. (2017) described a female newborn with a severe neuromuscular disorder. She had generalized hypotonia, congenital bone fractures, no spontaneous movements, and poor respiratory effort, and she died within the first days of life. A male sib born later had the same clinical presentation. Karyotyping and screening of several neuromuscular disease genes were negative.

paragraphs.text: Bohm et al. (2019) gave a clinical, histologic, and genetic description of 3 families with ASCC1-related disorder. All patients had severe prenatal-onset muscle weakness, neonatal hypotonia, arthrogryposis, and congenital bone fractures. Muscle biopsies from affected infants showed intense oxidative rims beneath the sarcolemma and scattered remnants of sarcomeres with enlarged Z-bands. The authors suggested that these changes could be a histopathologic hallmark of the disorder.

paragraphs.text: Knierim et al. (2016) found that the phenotype of prenatal-onset spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures was associated with mutations in either of 2 genes, TRIP4 or ASCC1. Both genes encode subunits of the activating signal cointegrator 1 (ASC-1) complex.

paragraphs.text: Knierim et al. (2016) studied affected individuals from 4 families with prenatal-onset spinal muscular atrophy and congenital bone fractures. Using autozygosity mapping and whole-exome sequencing, they identified homozygous and compound heterozygous nonsense and frameshift mutations in the TRIP4 and ASCC1 genes, which encode subunits of the nuclear ASC-1 complex. The mutations cosegregated with the disease and led to truncation or complete absence of the respective proteins. ASCC1-mutant patient fibroblasts showed downregulation of genes involved in neurogenesis and bone development (see PATHOGENESIS).

paragraphs.text: Oliveira et al. (2017) performed whole-exome sequencing under a recessive model in a female newborn with SMABF2, whose male sib had the same presentation. They first found no disease-causing variants in known neuromuscular genes. They then identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the ASCC1 gene (c.157dupG, p.Glu53GlyfsTer19) in the proband. The authors concluded that this second known case confirmed ASCC1 involvement in a severe neuromuscular disease within the spinal muscular atrophy or primary muscle disease spectrum.

paragraphs.text: Giuffrida et al. (2020) found compound heterozygous mutations in the ASCC1 gene in a stillborn fetus with SMABF2. Microarray analysis first detected a microdeletion of about 64 kb that involved 4 exons of ASCC1. Exome analysis then identified a c.1027C-T nonsense mutation (Arg343Ter) that introduces a premature termination codon. The authors stated that this was the first reported case of ASCC1 compound heterozygosity caused by an exonic microdeletion together with a nucleotide variant.

paragraphs.text: Knierim et al. (2016) found that ASCC1-mutant patient fibroblasts downregulated genes associated with neurogenesis, neuronal migration, and pathfinding (SERPINF1, DAB1, SEMA3D, SEMA3A) and genes associated with bone development (TNFRSF11B, RASSF2, STC1). Immunoprecipitation of the ASC-1 complex consistently copurified the transcriptional cofactor CSRP1. The authors concluded that dysfunction of a transcriptional coactivator complex can cause a syndrome that affects the neuromuscular system.

paragraphs.text: Oliveira et al. (2017) studied a female newborn with SMABF2 who died within the first days of life; a later-born male sib had the same presentation. In the proband they identified a homozygous 1-bp duplication (c.157dupG) in the ASCC1 gene, which causes a frameshift (Glu53GlyfsTer19). The variant was found by whole-exome sequencing under a recessive model after no disease-causing variants were found in known neuromuscular genes.

paragraphs.text: Exome analysis by Giuffrida et al. (2020) identified a c.1027C-T transition in the ASCC1 gene in a stillborn fetus with SMABF2, arthrogryposis, and hydrops. The change produces an arg343-to-ter (R343X) substitution and introduces a premature termination codon. The fetus was compound heterozygous for this mutation and a microdeletion of about 64 kb involving 4 exons of ASCC1.
